computer-vision.title: Teaching the confirmation stage to handle occlusion
computer-vision.summary: We’re retraining the confirmation stage on realistic, partially covered target crops so it can handle the difficult cases the detector sees at flight altitude.

body.text: With a lighter confirmation model in the works, we turned our attention to a common real-world headache: partially covered targets. A mannequin tucked under brush or a tent partly collapsed can still get flagged correctly by the detector, but the confirmation stage needs more practice recognizing these trickier cases.

We’re retraining the confirmation stage on crops that better reflect what the detector actually sees at flight altitude, with a stronger emphasis on partial-occlusion examples. Synthetic generation is proving especially useful here, since we can place targets under partial cover directly instead of waiting to find real-world examples of it.
Early signs are encouraging, and we’re feeling good about where the pipeline stands heading into our next round of outdoor testing.
Next up: fold these improvements into the full detector retrain and start planning our first full outdoor test of the complete search-to-confirmation loop.

computer-vision.title: Zeroing in on the real bottleneck
computer-vision.summary: End-to-end timing showed that detection is performing well; the heavier confirmation stage is where most of our processing time is going.

body.text: With the Jetson pipeline running smoothly, we finally timed the whole system end to end — and detection turned out not to be the slow part. The confirmation stage, which double-checks whether a detected region is really the mannequin, the tent, or just background clutter, is where most of our processing time is going.

Right now that stage relies on a heavier, general-purpose model, which is accurate but on the slower side for real-time use. We’re scoping out a lighter, purpose-built classifier to take its place, with an eye toward running it on the Jetson’s GPU alongside detection.
Good problem to have — it means the detector itself is performing well.
Next up: benchmark lighter classifier options and start looking at how it handles trickier real-world cases like partial occlusion.

computer-vision.title: Finding and fixing the rough edges
computer-vision.summary: Fixing small image-scaling and model-output mismatches brought Jetson detections in line with our bench results.

body.text: Spent this stretch chasing down some inconsistencies between our Jetson results and our bench results. Turned out to be a couple of small mismatches in how the pipeline was handling image scaling and how it was reading the model’s output — nothing structural, just details that needed lining up.
Once those were sorted, detections on the Jetson started matching what we’d seen during development, and confidence levels across both classes look solid.
We’re treating this as a good sign that the core pipeline is close to flight-ready, and we’re shifting focus to making sure the whole system runs quickly enough in real time.
Next up: get the full pipeline running on our test rig and start timing each stage, not just detection on its own.

computer-vision.title: Getting the model onto the Jetson
computer-vision.summary: We exported the YOLO model through TensorRT conversion so onboard inference can take advantage of the Jetson’s GPU.

body.text: This week was all about getting our YOLO model ready to run onboard. We exported the model and worked it through TensorRT conversion so it can take advantage of the Jetson’s GPU instead of relying on slower CPU inference.

There were a few hiccups along the way getting the converted model to behave the same way it did on our development machines, but nothing that pointed to a problem with the model itself — just the usual friction of getting a pipeline to run the same way on new hardware.
We’re optimistic about where this is headed and are looking forward to timing the full pipeline once everything is stable on-device.
Next up: finish smoothing out on-device performance and start timing the complete detection pipeline end to end.

computer-vision.title: Locking in our detection approach
computer-vision.summary: We settled on one YOLO model for both target classes and a synthetic-data pipeline that produces correctly scaled, automatically labelled training images.

body.text: This week we settled on our core detection strategy: a single YOLO model trained to recognize both the mannequin and the tent, rather than running two separate models. With everything else competing for compute onboard, one model handling both classes made the most sense for keeping things fast and simple.

To get there, we’re leaning heavily on synthetic data generation. Using SDXL inpainting, we’re placing targets into realistic pasture backgrounds matched to the Search Boundary terrain out at Skyway Range, Tulsa, with mask sizing tied to our camera’s ground sample distance so targets show up at the right scale for a given altitude. Because we control the placement, labels come out accurate automatically, which saves us a ton of manual annotation work down the line.
Early test renders are looking good, and we’re excited to start scaling this up into a full training set.
Next up: build out a larger batch of synthetic images and start looking at what it takes to get this running fast on the Jetson.

control.title: Control update: ICMTC 2026, 3rd place and best mission performance
control.summary: 3rd overall and best mission performance at ICMTC 2026. Mission 1 flew 1.72 km across 9 waypoints with a mid-mission payload drop at 0.12 m altitude RMSE.

body.text: We placed 3rd overall at ICMTC 2026 and took best mission performance. Mission 1 is the flight worth writing about.
It was a single-lap, 9-waypoint autonomous route with a mid-mission payload drop, flown on the same rate-controller gains from earlier in the season and the script stack described above.

body.heading: Mission 1
items: Duration: 538.2 s
Distance flown: 1.72 km
Max altitude: 46.99 m
Altitude tracking: 0.12 m RMSE, the tightest we saw all season
Waypoint accuracy: ~7.5 m average error, well inside the competition’s 30 m tolerance
Landed safely

body.text: Because if there’s one thing this flight proved, it’s that the controller isn’t the bottleneck anymore. 0.12 m of altitude tracking under real competition conditions is about as tight as it gets.

control.title: Control update: rules we now write every script around
control.summary: Retry loops on every critical call, clear_mission() before every upload, servo lock only after arm(). The list of rules we’d already paid for in debugging time.

body.text: Past a certain point this season we stopped treating each new mission script as fresh code and started treating it as an application of rules we’d already paid for in debugging time. The list:

Every critical MAVSDK call (arming, takeoff, mission upload, servo actuation) goes through a retry loop now, 3 to 5 attempts a couple of seconds apart. Nothing critical is allowed to fail silently on the first try, because on real hardware the first try sometimes just doesn’t land.

clear_mission() runs before every single upload. Skip it and the drone hangs in Hold mode after takeoff. That one cost us more debugging time than it should have before we traced it back to a stale mission still sitting on the flight controller.

The payload-release servo gets locked into its safe position immediately after arm() returns, never before. PX4 resets actuator outputs to a disarmed position the instant it arms, so an earlier lock just gets overwritten.

We call RTL manually instead of letting PX4 handle return-to-launch on its own after the mission. That gives us control over how the return flight lines up with payload sequencing rather than leaving the timing to the autopilot.

On the hardware side, ModemManager was quietly interfering with USB serial communication to the flight controller, so it’s permanently disabled on the companion Pi. And mavsdk_server gets restarted fresh before every test run, since stale connection state carrying over between runs was a recurring source of flaky behaviour that took a while to diagnose each time.
Nothing on this list is clever. It’s the reason the mission script held up on competition day without any of these old failure modes showing up again.

control.title: Control update: the bug that changed how we trigger payload release
control.summary: Mission-progress logs showed waypoints being skipped entirely. For a payload release gated on one waypoint event, that’s a release that might never fire.

body.text: One specific bug, with an outsized effect on how our mission scripts are structured.

Early versions of the payload-release logic hung off a waypoint-reached event. The script waited for the mission to report it had reached a particular waypoint, then triggered the release. Reasonable enough. Then we went through the mission-progress logs and found waypoints being skipped: the mission would report jumping from waypoint 2 straight to waypoint 4, with no waypoint 3 event logged at all.
For most of a mission that’s harmless. For a payload release gated on one specific waypoint event, it’s a release that might never fire.

The trigger now fires unconditionally once the mission-progress loop finishes, with no dependence on any single waypoint event along the way. Small change in the code. We only found it because we read the logs closely after a flight that looked fine from the ground.

control.title: Control update: why we stopped trusting the "obvious" API calls
control.summary: Three MAVSDK calls that look right in the documentation and fail on real hardware — and what we replaced each of them with.

body.text: Writing autonomous mission scripts for our companion computer taught us the same lesson several times over this season. The MAVSDK call that looks correct in the documentation is not always the one that works on real hardware. Three we tried, watched fail in flight, and dropped:

set_takeoff_altitude() went first. It’s the documented way to set a takeoff height and it’s known to be unreliable on real hardware. We set MIS_TAKEOFF_ALT directly through the parameter system instead, and that’s been solid ever since.

set_current_mission_item() went second. On paper it lets a script jump to a specific mission item on demand. On our hardware it timed out reliably, so we cut it rather than wrap retry logic around something that doesn’t work.

The third was a pattern rather than a function: waiting on altitude with a fixed asyncio.sleep(). A flat sleep can’t account for real variance in climb rate. Sometimes the aircraft is there early, sometimes late, and the fixed wait either burns time or moves on before the aircraft has arrived. Every altitude wait now polls against a tolerance band and only proceeds once the aircraft is actually where it needs to be.

These aren’t exotic bugs. They surface after you’ve flown the same script enough times on real hardware to see the pattern, which is also why they’re easy to relearn the hard way next season if nobody writes them down.

control.title: Control update: FRR, first flight at altitude
control.summary: A full dry run of the ICMTC mission plan, then FRR at meaningfully higher altitude than anything we’d tested at. Altitude tracking came in at 0.13 m RMSE.

body.text: Before FRR we ran a full dry run of the ICMTC competition mission plan, the same 9-waypoint route with the mid-mission payload drop we’d be flying later in the season. It ran clean, so we went into FRR fairly confident the mission logic wasn’t the risk. The unknown was altitude: meaningfully higher than anything we’d tested at.

Altitude doesn’t change the margin for error equally on every axis, so we didn’t scale everything up together. Takeoff altitude and horizontal cruise speed went up, because altitude and open air buy you room to react to a horizontal deviation. Vertical ascent and descent rates came down, because misjudging altitude up there is far less recoverable than drifting sideways. We also redid barometer and gyro calibration and tightened the actuator PWM range before the flight.

body.heading: Before → After
items: Takeoff altitude: 10 m → 17.98 m
Landing-approach altitude: 10 m → 20 m
Final landing-phase altitude: 5 m → 7 m
Cruise speed: 3 m/s → 5 m/s
Auto ascent rate: 3 m/s → 1.6 m/s
Auto descent rate: 1.5 m/s → 1.0 m/s

body.text: The flight reached 45.41 m, held a steady ~16 m cruise for most of the mission, and landed safely. Altitude tracking came in at 0.13 m RMSE, about as tight as anything we’d flown lower down. That was the answer we wanted: the gains generalized past the conditions we tuned them in.

control.title: Control update: first clean mission
control.summary: A deliberately small test — 3 waypoints and an automatic return-to-launch — to prove the new gains held up in the air rather than just on the bench.

body.text: With the new gains locked in, we needed to know whether the fix held up in the air and not just on the bench. The test was deliberately small: a 3-waypoint autonomous mission with an automatic return-to-launch.

It flew clean. Three waypoints, RTL, landing, no drama. Not much of a mission, but it was the first time we could call the oscillation fix flight-proven rather than a good-looking number on a vibration plot, and we tested a lot more aggressively after it.

control.title: Control update: taming "crazy flight"
control.summary: An oscillation across roll, pitch and yaw left Storm unsafe to fly. We reworked the rate-controller gains by hand against the flight logs instead of re-running AutoTune.

body.text: Most of this update was one problem: an oscillation we’d nicknamed "Crazy Flight." The aircraft shook across roll, pitch and yaw badly enough that it wasn’t safely flyable. We could have re-run PX4’s AutoTune and hoped for a better result. Instead we went through the rate-controller gains by hand and checked them against what the flight logs were actually showing.

body.heading: Where we ended up
items: Angle gains: roll/pitch P at 6.5, yaw P at 4.67

body.text: Oscillation on all three axes dropped by roughly half compared to where we started.

What took the longest was working out why AutoTune’s first pass made things worse in places. Its D-term can amplify structural resonance in the airframe rather than damp it out. So we kept the P and I terms, which do reflect real airframe response, and re-checked the D terms by hand against vibration data instead of trusting them blind. We treat AutoTune as a starting point now, not an answer.

electrical.title: Electrical Update: Power System Sizing
electrical.summary: This period, the electrical team focused on sizing the power system based on mechanical's estimated all-up weight of just under 7 kg with payload.

body.text: September 2025 – January 2026

This period, the electrical team focused on sizing the power system based on mechanical's estimated all-up weight of just under 7 kg with payload. We used a 2:1 thrust-to-weight ratio as our design floor, giving the aircraft enough margin to correct for gusts and hold altitude rather than just hover. At that weight, this comes out to roughly 14 kgf of total thrust, about 3.5 kgf per motor.

We also put together a power budget for the avionics stack — Pixhawk 6C, Holybro M9N GPS, RFD900A telemetry, RadioMaster ER8 receiver, SIYI A8 Mini, and Jetson Orin Nano — coming to about 35 W total. This rail is kept separate from the propulsion rail, since a voltage dip on the avionics side can reset the flight controller mid-flight.

During payload release testing, we ran 50 bench trials and got 47 clean releases. The 3 failures turned out to be a test setup issue: the servo was being bench-tested without an ESC in the loop, and it draws its power through the ESC's BEC rather than an independent rail. Once we added the ESC back into the test setup, all 3 released cleanly.

For the battery, we sized capacity based on average current draw over mission duration with a 20% margin added for wind, aggressive maneuvering, and cold-weather capacity loss. We also checked the pack's C-rating against peak current during a full-throttle climb, since a pack that's fine for average draw can still sag badly under peak load. We landed on a MAD 6S 28 Ah solid-state pack, rated for 140 A continuous and 280 A max.
Next steps: hand off thrust requirements to the propulsion trade study and begin motor thrust/current testing on the bench.

electrical.title: Electrical Update: Telemetry Calibration and Endurance Testing
electrical.summary: This period, we ran into an issue with our power module. The PM07 was reporting pack voltage and current that disagreed with a handheld meter.

body.text: February – May 2026

This period, we ran into an issue with our power module. The PM07 was reporting pack voltage and current that disagreed with a handheld meter. This module uses analog sensing with scaling constants that ship as generic defaults and need to be calibrated against a real meter — something we hadn't done yet, and the readings were especially unreliable at low current, right where our avionics rail sits.

This mattered because the low-battery failsafe is calculated from that current reading, so an inaccurate number meant our return-to-launch trigger point wasn't where we designed it to be. We started investigating whether to move to a module with factory-calibrated digital telemetry instead of maintaining our own calibration.

We also built an endurance model using our avionics power budget (35.4 W, ~1.59 A at 22.2 V) combined with per-motor current at takeoff, cruise, and landing, budgeting 80% of the pack's rated capacity as usable. This gave us an estimated flight time of around 30 minutes — a bench-derived estimate we still needed to confirm in flight.

To get a real number for the ESCs, we bench-tested each Avenger 4215 V5 motor to full throttle and measured 61.5 A per motor at the takeoff operating point. We paired these with Hobbywing Skywalker 80 A V2 ESCs, giving about 30% current headroom above the measured worst case, and sized our wiring (10 AWG battery leads, 8 AWG PM08-CAN leads) against the full four-motor worst case of 246 A.
Next steps: test sustained full-throttle operation over a longer duration, and fly a timed endurance test to check against our 30-minute estimate.

electrical.title: Electrical Update: Power Module Failure and Redesign
electrical.summary: After a full mission-profile test flight, we noticed smoke coming from the PM07's buck regulator shortly after landing, while the battery was still connected.

body.text: June 2026

After a full mission-profile test flight, we noticed smoke coming from the PM07's buck regulator shortly after landing, while the battery was still connected. We disconnected the battery immediately. No other components on that rail were damaged.

Our working theory is thermal: the PM07 is rated for 90 A continuous with no forced airflow, and while hover current stays well within that rating, a full mission with real climbs and corrections is a more demanding duty cycle. We didn't have current logging in place at the time, so we can't confirm the exact current at failure.

Looking back, we'd already measured 246 A as our four-motor worst case back in May, and the PM07's 90 A rating was on record separately — but the two numbers were never compared directly until this failure.

We replaced the power distribution setup with a 300 A side-entry PDB for propulsion and a PM08-CAN (200 A continuous) for sensing, sized against the measured worst case rather than typical hover load. The PM08-CAN also reports over DroneCAN instead of analog sensing, giving us factory-calibrated telemetry and removing the scaling-constant issue from the earlier update.
After the swap, we confirmed voltage and current readings matched a handheld meter without calibration, and tested the full rail under simultaneous load on the bench before reintegration.

Final architecture: a single MAD 6S 28 Ah pack feeding the PM08-CAN (powering the Pixhawk 6C, telemetry radio, receiver, GPS, and release servo) and the 300 A PDB (powering the four ESCs, gimbal, and — via a buck converter — the Jetson Orin Nano). Avionics and propulsion remain on physically separate rails.
Next steps: reintegrate into the airframe and document the finalized rail assignments.

electrical.title: Electrical Update: Wiring Incident and Process Changes
electrical.summary: During reintegration of the new power module, a positive and negative terminal made contact and caused a short.

body.text: July 2026

During reintegration of the new power module, a positive and negative terminal made contact and caused a short. The battery stopped holding charge afterward, reading close to zero volts, and was taken out of service.
This happened during routine reintegration work, not during anything unusual, which is generally when this kind of incident happens.

As a result, we made several changes to our wiring process: exposed terminals and bus bars are now insulated with heat-shrink or tape before any integration work begins, connections are made one polarity at a time wherever possible, and polarity is checked with a multimeter on any new or modified harness before it's connected. We also wrote down and rehearsed a battery disconnect procedure for the team.

More broadly, we're now logging voltage and current on every flight, since the lack of logging made it hard to diagnose the June regulator failure. Components are sized against measured worst-case draw rather than typical draw, with that number recorded alongside the part selection. And any servo or actuator system gets bench-tested with its real power path (ESC included) before flight, a lesson from earlier payload testing that's held up throughout the season.
Next steps: fly the timed endurance test that's been pending since March, now that telemetry is reliable enough to trust the result.

mechanical.title: Storm is airframe-complete
mechanical.summary: Airframe build is done — 5 kg quadrotor-X, 4.09:1 thrust-to-weight, and it folds down small enough to fit a personal-item bag.

body.text: Called the airframe build complete this week. Storm comes in at 5 kg without payload — a from-scratch quadrotor-X built specifically around the five SUAS 2026 mission tasks instead of adapting an off-the-shelf frame.

body.heading: Where the numbers landed
items: Four Avenger 4215 V5 motors, each rated for 6902 g static thrust, against a 6750 g all-up weight including payload — 4.09:1 max thrust-to-weight.
Folded footprint: 18 × 14 × 8 in, small enough to travel in a personal-item bag for the Design for Rapid Response task.
That thrust margin is there for gust rejection in wind up to 14 mph and reserve authority during payload drop maneuvers, not just for looking good on paper.

body.text: Airframe done just means it's ready for the next round of flight testing — haven't pushed it anywhere near that 14 mph gust number in real conditions yet.

mechanical.title: Landing gear failed the drop test — here's what we changed
mechanical.summary: First landing gear design cracked on a 2 m drop test. Redesigned it, dropped it again, and it held.

body.text: Ran the landing gear through a 2 m drop test and it failed on impact. Not the outcome we wanted, but exactly why we test before committing to a design.
Reworked the leg geometry and rebuilt it, then dropped it from the same 2 m height again. This time it held with no visible damage.

body.heading: Same day, motor mount test
items: Ran all four motors at full throttle for a sustained 1-minute ground test.
No deformation, no loosened fasteners, no mount failure observed afterward.
Full FEA factor-of-safety analysis is still running in parallel — the physical test passing doesn't mean we skip that step.

body.text: Next: repeat the landing gear drop test from a greater height to find where the new design actually fails, instead of just confirming it clears the minimum bar.

mechanical.title: Locking the frame material and mass budget
mechanical.summary: Went with sandwich composite plates after tracking mass at the component level — battery and payload alone are 39% of AUW.

body.text: Tracked mass line by line at the component level this cycle instead of just weighing finished assemblies, and it paid off — the battery and payload together account for roughly 39% of all-up weight. That's a big enough chunk that it drove material decisions everywhere else on the frame.

Went with sandwich composite construction for the structural plates: a 600 g fiberglass core between two multi-directional carbon fiber face layers. Gets close to solid carbon fiber stiffness-to-weight without the full material cost, which matters when the battery and payload are already eating that much of the budget.

body.heading: Manufacturing notes
items: Built a full-scale mockup before committing to composite manufacturing, just to catch dimension and fitment issues cheaply.
Frame plates are cut by an outsourced composites shop using vacuum bagging, then CNC-finished to final geometry.
Arms are carbon fiber for the same stiffness-to-weight reasoning as the plates.

body.text: Next: lock the mockup-validated dimensions with the composites shop and start on the actual production plates.

mechanical.title: Two release mechanisms, one drop test day
mechanical.summary: Trap door for the flare, bracket latch for the water bottle — first drop tests landed within 30–75 ft of target from 10 m.

body.text: Built two separate release mechanisms since the two payloads don't behave the same way: a servo-actuated trap door for the flare, and a servo-driven bracket latch for the water bottle. Looked at a winch-based delivery system for both early on but dropped it — extra weight and slower deployment time than a 45-minute mission window can really afford.

body.heading: First drop test results
items: All test drops released cleanly from both mechanisms.
Impact points landed within 30 to 75 ft of the target from a 10 m drop altitude — usable, but a wider spread than we want for competition scoring.
Custom non-structural mounts (landing gear connectors, GPS mount, payload housing, camera bracket) are all FDM-printed in PLA+, holding up fine through this round of testing.

body.text: 30–75 ft is too wide a spread to call this done. Next iteration needs tighter release timing or a better drop-point calculation, not just repeated tests of the same setup.

mechanical.title: Motor and prop trade study — three options down to one
mechanical.summary: Bench-compared three motor options and two props before settling on the Avenger 4215 V5 and the 15558 folding tri-blade.

body.text: Bench-tested three motor candidates before picking one. The AT4125 Long Shaft pulled 72 A at full throttle versus 61.5 A for the Avenger 4215 V5 — worse on current draw and more expensive, an easy cut. The T-Motor U7 V2.0 got ruled out too, mostly on cost and because it doesn't fold down well for transport.

Prop comparison came down to two folding tri-blades. The 1248 only made 6676 g of thrust per motor at 3.21 g/W, while the 15558 hit 6902 g at 3.79 g/W — more thrust and meaningfully better efficiency, so that one was the clear pick.

body.heading: Other changes made off the back of this round
items: Motor arms switched from aluminum to carbon fiber for better strength-to-weight over the previous platform.
Landing gear stance widened for better lateral stability landing in gusty conditions.

body.text: Next: get the selected motor/prop combo mounted on the actual airframe and re-run the thrust-current bench test in that configuration, not just on the test stand.
